content:
Quick answer: Arthritis alone does not need reporting. GOV.UK says you must tell the DVLA if you use special controls for driving, or if your arthritis affects your ability to drive safely. You can be fined up to £1,000 if you do not. Check with your doctor about painkillers such as codeine, and wait at least 6 weeks after a hip or total knee replacement.

Checked on 10 October 2026 against GOV.UK and DVLA guidance on arthritis and driving, medical conditions, disabilities and driving and drugs and driving, GOV.UK guidance on vehicle tax, Motability and Blue Badges, NHS joint replacement recovery advice, and Driving Mobility. Rules can change, so check the linked pages before you act.

For many people with arthritis, driving is what keeps work, appointments, shopping and friendships within reach. The good news is that most people with arthritis can keep driving safely, often with small changes to the car or how they drive. This guide explains exactly when the law says you must tell the DVLA, how your medicines and any surgery affect driving, and the practical and financial help available.

Do I need to tell the DVLA about my arthritis?

Having arthritis does not on its own mean you must tell the DVLA. The GOV.UK page on arthritis and driving says that if you have a car or motorcycle licence, you must tell the DVLA if you use special controls for driving, such as adapted steering, hand controls or a left-foot accelerator. You can report online or by filling in form G1.

More generally, GOV.UK says you must tell the DVLA if you develop a condition or disability that could affect your ability to drive safely, or if an existing condition gets worse. If you are not sure whether your arthritis affects your driving, or whether you need to tell the DVLA, GOV.UK advises talking to your doctor.

  • Fines: you can be fined up to £1,000 if you do not tell the DVLA about a medical condition that affects your driving, and you could be prosecuted if you have an accident as a result.
  • Bus, coach or lorry licence: the same principle applies, but you use form G1V and higher medical standards apply.
  • Northern Ireland: you contact the Driver and Vehicle Agency (DVA) instead of the DVLA.
  • Aged 70 or over: you must declare notifiable conditions when you renew your licence, on the application form.

Telling the DVLA does not automatically mean losing your licence. The DVLA decides whether you can keep driving, sometimes with conditions such as a licence for adapted vehicles only.

When you must stop driving

GOV.UK says you must surrender your licence to the DVLA if your doctor tells you to stop driving for 3 months or more, if your condition affects your ability to drive safely and lasts 3 months or more, or if you do not meet the required medical standards. You can apply to get your licence back when you meet the standards again.

A quick self-check before you drive

Arthritis can change from day to day. Before driving, especially during a flare, ask yourself honestly whether you can:

  • grip and turn the steering wheel quickly and fully, including when parking
  • press the brake hard enough and fast enough for an emergency stop
  • turn your head and upper body to check blind spots and reverse
  • use the handbrake, gearstick, indicators and wipers without pain stopping you
  • get in and out of the car safely
  • concentrate fully, without pain, tiredness or medicines making you drowsy

If the answer to any of these is no, do not drive that day. Have a back-up plan for flare days, such as a lift, a taxi, public transport or a remote appointment.

Medicines and driving

GOV.UK says it is illegal in England, Scotland and Wales to drive with legal drugs in your body if they impair your driving. It lists medicines to talk to your doctor about before driving, including morphine and other opioids such as codeine, tramadol and fentanyl, and benzodiazepines such as diazepam.

You can drive after taking these if they have been prescribed, you follow the advice on how to take them, and they are not making you unfit to drive. The law does not cover Northern Ireland, but you could still be arrested there if you are unfit to drive.

Practical steps:

  • Read the patient information leaflet. Many pain and sleep medicines carry warnings about drowsiness.
  • Be extra careful when you start a medicine, change the dose or combine it with alcohol.
  • Keep your prescription or a repeat slip with you in case you are stopped.
  • Ask your pharmacist if you are not sure whether a medicine affects driving. Our guide to anti-inflammatory painkillers covers safe use of common pain relief.

Driving after joint replacement

NHS guidance says to wait at least 6 weeks to drive after a hip replacement or total knee replacement, and at least 3 weeks after a partial knee replacement, and to check with your doctor that you are fit to drive. You need to be able to control the car safely, including an emergency stop.

  • You do not normally need to tell the DVLA about a short recovery period, but the surrender rule above applies if your doctor says not to drive for 3 months or more.
  • Tell your insurer you have had surgery and check their rules, as some have their own requirements.
  • Plan transport for the first weeks before your operation. See our guide to preparing for joint replacement.

Car features and adaptations that can help

Many helpful features are now standard on new and used cars. Things to look for or ask about:

  • Automatic gearbox, which removes the clutch pedal and gear changes
  • Keyless entry and push-button start, so you do not need to turn a small key
  • Electric parking brake instead of a lever
  • Light power steering, parking sensors and a reversing camera, which reduce twisting
  • Seat height and adjustable lumbar support, so getting in and out is easier
  • Heated seats and steering wheel, which some people find comfortable for stiff joints
  • Wide door openings and a higher seating position

Small aids such as a swivel cushion, a steering wheel cover with a thicker grip, a key turner or a seat belt reacher can also help. Our guide to gadgets and aids for arthritis has more ideas.

Larger adaptations, such as hand controls, steering aids or a left-foot accelerator, need specialist fitting and must be reported to the DVLA because they count as special controls.

Get a professional driving assessment

Driving Mobility is a network of independent driving and mobility assessment centres across the UK. They offer assessments that look at what you can do, which car features or adaptations would help, and whether you can drive safely. They also offer refresher courses and advice on alternatives to driving. The charity's website explains how to find a centre and apply for its Drivers Assessment Grant towards the cost of an assessment and adaptations.

A driving assessment can be especially useful if you are returning to driving after a long break, surgery or a big change in your arthritis.

Car insurance

Tell your car insurer about any condition you have reported to the DVLA, any adaptations to your car and any recent surgery. If you do not, your insurer could refuse to pay a claim. Under the Equality Act 2010, insurers can only treat you differently because of a disability if this is based on relevant and reliable information about risk. If you feel you have been treated unfairly, the Financial Ombudsman Service is free to use.

Financial help with driving

Vehicle tax exemption or reduction

GOV.UK says you can claim exemption from vehicle tax for one vehicle if you get the enhanced rate mobility component of Personal Independence Payment (PIP) or Adult Disability Payment (ADP) in Scotland, or the higher rate mobility component of Disability Living Allowance (DLA). You can get a 50% reduction if you get the standard rate mobility component of PIP or ADP. The vehicle must be used for the disabled person's needs.

The Motability Scheme

The Motability Scheme lets you use your qualifying mobility allowance to lease a car, powered wheelchair or scooter. GOV.UK lists eligible allowances, including the enhanced rate mobility component of PIP or ADP and the higher rate mobility component of DLA. Motability says insurance, servicing and breakdown cover are included in the lease. You can find out more on the Motability website.

VAT relief

You may not have to pay VAT on adapting a vehicle to suit your condition, or on leasing a Motability vehicle, according to GOV.UK.

If you are thinking of applying for PIP, our PIP and benefits guide explains the process.

Blue Badges

A Blue Badge lets you park closer to where you need to go if you have severe walking difficulties, whether you drive or travel as a passenger. GOV.UK says:

  • A Blue Badge costs up to £10 in England and £20 in Scotland, and is free in Wales.
  • Badges usually last up to 3 years, and you must reapply before yours expires.
  • You can apply online if you live in England or Wales. Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own application services.
  • Your council usually makes a decision within 12 weeks.

Some people get a badge automatically through certain benefits; others are assessed by the council. Our guide to the Blue Badge and arthritis explains the criteria.

Making journeys more comfortable

  • Set up the seat properly. Sit so you can fully press the pedals with a slight bend in your knee, and reach the wheel without stretching.
  • Plan breaks. Stop every hour or so to stretch, walk and loosen stiff joints, more often during a flare.
  • Warm up first. A few gentle movements for your neck, shoulders, hands and knees before setting off can help with morning stiffness.
  • Choose your times. Avoid driving when you are most stiff or tired, and avoid rush hour where you can.
  • Refuelling and charging. Look for fuel stations that offer assistance, and keep a pair of gloves in the car to protect sore hands.
  • Keep essentials within reach, such as water, medicines, a cushion and a phone charger.

If you need to drive less, or stop

Giving up driving, even temporarily, can feel like a big loss. GOV.UK points to help such as an older person's or disabled person's bus pass, the Disabled Persons Railcard, and local dial-a-ride or taxi voucher schemes run by councils. Community transport schemes may help with hospital appointments. Driving Mobility offers advice for families on alternatives to driving.

If you voluntarily give up your licence, you can usually reapply when your health allows, subject to DVLA checks.

If a relative is worried about your driving

Sometimes family notice changes first, such as difficulty turning to reverse or getting in and out of the car. It can help to agree in advance how you will talk about it, and to treat a professional driving assessment as a neutral way to get an expert view rather than a test you could fail. A GP or specialist can also advise. Decisions about whether you can hold a licence are made by the DVLA, not by family members.

When to get medical help

Speak to your GP or specialist team if your arthritis is making it harder to drive safely, if you are worried about a new medicine, or if you need advice on whether to tell the DVLA. Get urgent help from NHS 111 or your GP the same day if you have a hot, swollen, very painful joint with a fever, or sudden weakness or numbness in your legs. Call 999 if you have sudden weakness on one side, slurred speech, or chest pain.

Frequently asked questions

Do I have to tell the DVLA I have arthritis?

Not automatically. GOV.UK says you must tell the DVLA if you use special controls for driving, or if your arthritis affects your ability to drive safely. Talk to your doctor if you are not sure.

Can I drive after a hip or knee replacement?

NHS guidance says to wait at least 6 weeks after a hip or total knee replacement, or 3 weeks after a partial knee replacement, and to check with your doctor that you are fit to drive.

Is it illegal to drive on codeine or tramadol?

Not if they are prescribed, you take them as advised and they do not impair your driving. It is illegal to drive if any medicine makes you unfit to drive.

Will my insurance go up if I tell them about arthritis?

It depends on the insurer. Not telling them could invalidate your cover, so it is important to be honest.

Who can get the Motability Scheme?

People getting a qualifying mobility allowance, such as the enhanced rate mobility component of PIP or ADP, or the higher rate mobility component of DLA.

Can I get a driving assessment?

Yes. Driving Mobility centres across the UK offer assessments and advice on adaptations. Ask about their grant scheme if cost is a barrier.

Where do I report a condition in Northern Ireland?

To the Driver and Vehicle Agency (DVA), not the DVLA.
